query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr can be reduced without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures by substituting a portion of the heavier elements with lighter elements, such as replacing some of the Ta with Ti, while maintaining the high-entropy alloy composition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.intervention: Substitution of a portion of the heavier elements with lighter elements
generation.mechanism: The substitution of heavier elements with lighter elements reduces the overall density of the alloy while maintaining its mechanical properties due to the preservation of the high-entropy alloy composition, which provides strength and stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced density without sacrificing mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of substitution required to achieve the desired reduction in density without compromising mechanical properties is uncertain and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of HfMoTaTiZr with varying levels of substitution of heavier elements with lighter elements, and test their mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Mechanical properties (e.g., strength, hardness) at room temperature and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substitution of heavier elements with lighter elements results in a significant decrease in mechanical properties at room temperature or elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
